headline: Microsoft moves Copilot's Deep Research and other features behind a $19.99/month subscription
summary: Microsoft is merging its Copilot apps, removing several free features like Deep Research, Podcasts, and Group Chat. The Deep Research successor, "Researcher," now requires a Microsoft 365 Premium subscription, reportedly costing $19.99 monthly.
details: Microsoft began retiring several free consumer features in Copilot as of August 18, including the popular Deep Research tool. This change comes as the company consolidates its Copilot applications.
The most impactful change is that Deep Research's successor, "Researcher," is now exclusive to paid Microsoft 365 Premium subscribers. This plan is reportedly priced at $19.99 per month.

As part of merging its consumer Copilot app with the business-oriented Microsoft 365 Copilot app, Microsoft also cut Group Chat, AI-generated Podcasts, Copilot Labs, and the animated Mico character. Free chat and image generation capabilities remain available.

Users with content in removed features, such as Podcasts, were required to manually download their data before the August 18 deadline. Failure to do so means their content is no longer accessible within the app.

Existing Deep Research reports are not deleted; Premium subscribers can access them through Researcher, while Personal and Family subscribers can find previous reports in their chat history. All reports can also be saved to Microsoft Word, offering a gentler transition for users.

headline_marked: [[DHS uses obscure customs law]] to snoop on journalists, non-profits, and unions without judicial oversight
headline: DHS uses obscure customs law to snoop on journalists, non-profits, and unions without judicial oversight
summary: The Trump administration deployed an arcane federal law, 19 USC 1509, typically for customs inspections, to bypass judges and obtain private data, including journalist phone records.
details: The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) under the Trump administration used an obscure customs law (19 USC 1509) to obtain private information on journalists, non-profits, and unions. This tactic allowed DHS to bypass judicial oversight, raising significant alarm among legal experts.

In one notable case, DHS obtained six months of telephone records for Minneapolis journalist Georgia Fort, including over 10,000 calls and text messages, from T-Mobile. Fort was not notified of this request until months later, after the records were produced to her lawyers.

Earlier, federal prosecutors had twice sought search warrants for YouTube account information for Fort and journalist Don Lemon, who faced criminal charges related to covering a protest. A judge rejected these requests, citing a lack of probable cause and the need for the journalists to be informed.

Despite the judicial rejections, DHS subsequently served Google with an administrative summons for the same YouTube information, using the customs law. This method only required a sign-off from a DHS official, effectively circumventing the judge's prior ruling.

Former DHS lawyer Chris Duncan stated these laws "have absolutely nothing to do with a domestic situation at a church, a social media post, even an immigration matter." Former DHS Inspector General John Roth called it an "improper use of the subpoena."

Beyond Fort and Lemon, DHS also sought YouTube account information for Democracy Now, conservative podcaster Megyn Kelly, the Milwaukee Journal-Sentinel, and independent journalist Brendan Gutenschwager. The summons instructed recipients to keep the request secret.

Concerns are high that such actions could be used to uncover journalists' confidential sources, undermining press freedom. T-Mobile stated it reviews government demands in accordance with the law but declined to comment on specific cases.
